1: The Moon is about 384,000 km from Earth, almost like flying around our planet 10 times.
2: The first people stepped on the Moon on July 20, 1969: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin of Apollo 11.
3: The Moon is about 3,474 km across, roughly a quarter of Earth's width.
4: You can't hear any sound on the Moon because there is no air, so astronauts talk by radio.
5: The Sun always blows a solar wind: a stream of particles moving at about 400 km per second.
6: The Sun is so big that about 1.3 million Earths could fit inside it.
7: The surface of the Sun is about 5,500 °C hot.
8: The Sun weighs more than everything else in the Solar System put together: it has 99.8% of all the mass.
9: The Sun is about 4.5 billion years old, which is about halfway through its life.
10: The SOHO space observatory has been watching the Sun since 1995 and sees plasma clouds flying into space.
11: In the daytime the Moon's surface heats up to about 127 °C, hotter than boiling water.
12: The dark patches on the Moon are called "seas", but there is no water there: they are old, frozen lava.
13: Craters on the Moon were made by asteroid impacts, and with no wind or rain they last for billions of years.
14: The Moon doesn't glow by itself: we see sunlight bouncing off its surface.
15: In 1968 the Apollo 8 crew photographed Earth rising over the Moon, and the photo was named "Earthrise".
16: The Moon has moonquakes: they were recorded by instruments that the Apollo astronauts left behind.
17: Parker Solar Probe flies closer to the Sun than any other spacecraft and is the fastest object people have ever built.
18: Between 1969 and 1972, 12 astronauts walked on the Moon.
19: Apollo astronauts brought 382 kg of Moon rocks and dust back to Earth.
20: Moon dust is sharp and sticky, like tiny bits of glass, so it clings to spacesuits and machines.
21: On the Moon you can jump about 6 times higher than on Earth, so astronauts hopped like kangaroos.
22: Every year the Moon moves about 3.8 cm farther from Earth, almost as fast as your fingernails grow.
23: The ocean tides on Earth are caused by the pull of the Moon.
24: Green and red auroras glow because of oxygen, and blue and purple ones because of nitrogen in the air.
25: There is ice in dark craters near the Moon's south pole, where sunlight never reaches.
26: The Moon most likely formed 4.5 billion years ago when a Mars-sized body crashed into the young Earth.
27: The nearest star after the Sun is Proxima Centauri, and its light takes more than 4 years to reach us.
28: NASA has space weather forecasters who watch the Sun to keep astronauts on future Artemis missions safe.
29: With the Artemis program, NASA plans to land people on the Moon again, this time near its south pole.
30: The Apollo astronauts' footprints are still on the Moon, because there is no wind to blow them away.
